title: Spoken Language Foundations Adventure
welcome_lead: Today you'll meet the key terms for studying how people actually speak.
meta_desc: GCSE English Language spoken language walkthrough — Standard English, dialect, accent, sociolect.
final_note: You learned the difference between accent, dialect, sociolect and idiolect — and what Standard English really is.

concepts.def: Words and grammar typical of a region
Language variety of a social group
An individual person's unique way of speaking

walkthroughs.body_html:
Accent = how you say words. Dialect = which words and grammar you use.

A Yorkshire dialect speaker might say 'I were going up t' shop' — both grammar AND vocab differ.

Standard English isn't 'correct' English — it's just the variety used in writing, news and schools.

All other varieties are equally rule-governed.

Sociolect: a group's language (e.g. teen slang, legal jargon).

Idiolect: YOUR unique mix — your favourite phrases, fillers, sayings.

mcqs.q: Saying 'bath' with a short 'a' rather than a long one is a feature of:
options: Dialect
Accent
Sociolect
Idiolect

mcqs.q: Which is an example of an idiolect feature?
options: Cockney rhyming slang
Geordie dialect words
Your dad's constant 'right then'
Standard English grammar
A semantic field is a list of synonyms for one word.
Transitive verbs end in -ed and intransitive in -ing.
A group of words from a similar area of meaning — e.g. 'whisper, scream, mumble, shout' all belong to the semantic field of vocalisation.
A semantic field is a field of study like physics or biology.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between transitive and intransitive verbs?
options: A semantic field is a field of study like physics or biology.
Transitive verbs are action verbs and intransitive are linking verbs.
Transitive verbs end in -ed and intransitive in -ing.
Transitive verbs take a direct object ('she ate the cake'); intransitive verbs don't ('she slept'). Some verbs are both depending on use ('she ran' / 'she ran the company').
A syntactic unit headed by a noun, which may include determiners, adjectives and modifiers — e.g. 'the big red car' is a noun phrase functioning as a single grammatical unit.
A noun phrase is just a noun by itself.
Transitive verbs end in -ed and intransitive in -ing.
A noun phrase is a sentence that contains nouns.
